title: Early farmers from across Europe directly descended from Neolithic Aegeans
authors: Hofmanová, Z., Kreutzer, S., Hellenthal, G. et al.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (White Rose Research Online record)
ask_addressed: What do ancient DNA and archaeology show about the spread of farming from the Fertile Crescent into Europe and beyond (migration versus cultural diffusion), and the spread of bronze and iron working, the horse and wheeled vehicles, and Austronesian seafaring?
quote: Our study demonstrates a direct genetic link between Mediterranean and Central European early farmers and those of Greece and Anatolia
summary: Genomes of five Neolithic individuals from northern Greece and northwestern Turkey are genetically close to early farmers across Europe, which the authors read as a chain of migration from southwestern Asia.

title: Ancient cattle genomics, origins, and rapid turnover in the Fertile Crescent
authors: Verdugo, M.P., Mullin, V.E., Scheu, A. et al.
venue: Science (White Rose Research Online accepted version)
ask_addressed: What do ancient DNA and archaeology show about the spread of farming from the Fertile Crescent into Europe and beyond (migration versus cultural diffusion), and the spread of bronze and iron working, the horse and wheeled vehicles, and Austronesian seafaring?
quote: Ancient Near Eastern cattle show ancestry from multiple aurochs strains plus a massive zebu influx at the onset of the Meghalayan Age.
summary: Genomes of 67 ancient Near Eastern cattle show a region-wide Bronze Age shift from Indus zebu introgression, an animal (not people) transfer; the same study dates cattle domestication to about 10,500 BP in the Upper Euphrates and Tigris.
limits: Accepted manuscript. Concerns animal ancestry; the human carrier and route are inferred, not shown. The 4.2 ka drought link is the authors' proposal.

title: Bronze Age population dynamics and the rise of dairy pastoralism on the eastern Eurasian steppe
authors: Jeong, C., Wilkin, S., Amgalantugs, T. et al.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (White Rose Research Online)
ask_addressed: What do ancient DNA and archaeology show about the spread of farming from the Fertile Crescent into Europe and beyond (migration versus cultural diffusion), and the spread of bronze and iron working, the horse and wheeled vehicles, and Austronesian seafaring?
quote: ruminant dairy pastoralism was adopted on the Eastern steppe by local hunter-gatherers through a process of cultural transmission and minimal genetic exchange
summary: Milk proteins in dental calculus and genomes from Mongolia show dairy herding on the eastern steppe by 1300 BCE with little western steppe ancestry: a case of cultural diffusion without major migration.

title: Palaeopathology and horse domestication: the case of some Iron Age horses from the Altai Mountains, Siberia
authors: Levine, M.A., Bailey, G.N., Whitwell, K.E., Jeffcott, L.B.
venue: Human Ecodynamics, Oxbow Books (White Rose Research Online)
ask_addressed: Which parts are settled and which disputed?
quote: new radiocarbon dates for the Dereivka teeth have disproved the claims for early horse domestication at that site
summary: A sceptical zooarchaeological source on bit-wear and morphological indicators of horse domestication, reporting that redating undid the Dereivka claim.
limits: Published 2000, so it predates the genomic work; the Botai debate is not addressed. It argues that bit wear and kill-off patterns are ambiguous, not that horses were not domesticated later.

ask_addressed: What do ancient DNA and archaeology show about the spread of farming from the Fertile Crescent into Europe and beyond (migration versus cultural diffusion), and the spread of bronze and iron working, the horse and wheeled vehicles, and Austronesian seafaring?
quote: Current evidence supports an Anatolian origin for extractive iron metallurgy on a limited scale sometime in the early 2nd millennium BC.
summary: Review synthesising field, textual and archaeometric data: limited iron smelting in Anatolia early in the 2nd millennium BC, with large-scale expansion across the Near East only in the late 2nd and early 1st millennium BC.
